task.goal: Investigate why a paper-based package becomes damp in storage using safe bench observations rather than assuming the new coating failed.
hard_constraints: Ten sample packages, humidity logger and one week; no hazardous chemicals or customer shipments.
Distinguish ambient humidity, condensation and package material effects.
Do not claim causal proof from a single uncontrolled comparison.
task.available_resources: A dry cabinet and ordinary room storage.
task.expected_result: Competing explanations and bounded discriminating tests.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Humidity-response reversal: test whether dampness tracks storage air
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Primary mechanism: paper absorbs water vapor as ambient relative humidity rises and releases it in drier air. This can make packaging feel damp without a coating defect. Competing explanations are condensation during temperature changes and material-specific retention or absorption.

Number all ten packages and record their initial appearance, storage history if known, and dampness using a consistent descriptive scale. Photograph the same faces, seams and corners under similar lighting. Randomly assign five packages to the dry cabinet and five to ordinary room storage, keeping spacing and orientation comparable. After three days, exchange the groups and observe through day seven. Avoid placing packages near heaters, vents or wet surfaces.

Use the logger to document both environments in scheduled blocks, recording every relocation. One logger cannot measure both environments simultaneously; sequential readings therefore characterize conditions rather than provide a complete exposure record. If it records temperature, retain those readings too. No chemicals or shipment trials are needed.

The discriminating feature is reversibility: dampness that repeatedly develops in the room and diminishes in the cabinet supports humidity-dependent uptake. Persistent differences between packages under similar exposure suggest material or construction effects. Sudden droplets after movement suggest condensation instead.

Assumptions include a genuinely drier cabinet and packages with comparable contents and handling. Drying can remove both absorbed moisture and condensed water, so cabinet improvement alone cannot identify the original mechanism. Visual and tactile observations also lack the sensitivity of moisture-content measurements.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: The smallest useful check is the crossover itself: compare each package before and after changing environments against packages moving in the opposite direction. Observe twice daily and immediately after transfers. Failure to follow the destination environment weakens a simple ambient-humidity explanation. A single crossover remains exploratory because time, carryover and temperature changes are not fully controlled; report individual trajectories and competing interpretations rather than causal proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Transfer-event observation: look specifically for condensation
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Primary mechanism: a package surface colder than the surrounding air’s dew point collects liquid water. Condensation predicts a rapid, transfer-associated event, whereas vapor absorption generally produces a slower change and material effects may concentrate dampness at particular features.

First determine whether ordinary storage and the dry cabinet naturally differ in temperature. Do not introduce refrigeration, steam or artificial temperature shocks. If the logger measures temperature and relative humidity, record conditions in each location before moving packages. Air measurements can indicate condensation risk, but they do not establish actual package surface temperature. If temperature is unavailable, retain condensation as an observational hypothesis with correspondingly weaker discrimination.

Use four packages as transfer samples, three as room-stationary comparators and three as cabinet-stationary comparators. After two days of conditioning, move the transfer samples from whichever location is naturally cooler into the warmer location, provided that transfer is representative of plausible storage handling. Inspect immediately before movement, then at approximately five, fifteen, thirty and sixty minutes, and later that day. Repeat once later in the week if a similar natural temperature difference occurs.

Record visible droplets, sheen, localized wet patches and their disappearance, with photographs and minimal touching. Also note whether dampness emerges slowly in stationary packages. Material differences can alter where condensate collects or how long it remains, so localized wetness does not itself indict the coating.

This approach requires only the ten packages, logger, existing storage locations and observation time. Its main prerequisite is a naturally occurring temperature contrast. Without one, the week may provide no meaningful condensation challenge; that is an inconclusive test, not evidence excluding condensation.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare the four transferred packages with stationary packages observed at the same times. Rapid wetting confined to transferred samples supports a transfer-related explanation; similar slow changes across stationary and transferred packages weaken it. Repeatability strengthens the observation, but handling and humidity changes remain confounders. Without surface-temperature measurement, describe condensation as supported or unresolved, never proven from calculated air conditions alone.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Within-package moisture mapping: test material and construction effects
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Primary mechanism: different package regions absorb, transport or retain moisture differently. Exposed paper edges, folds, seams and adhesive areas may become damp before coated panels even when all experience approximately the same air. This tests whether package architecture helps explain dampness without presuming that the new coating failed.

Give every package a fixed observation map: broad panel, fold, seam, cut edge and base, wherever those features exist. Photograph and score the same locations at baseline. Note visible damage, contact with shelving and any pre-existing stains. Do not cut packages apart, add liquids or apply chemicals.

Randomly assign five packages to ordinary room storage and five to the dry cabinet for the week. Within each location, use comparable spacing and alternate package orientation; rotate positions midway through the week. Record changes in which face contacts the shelf. This helps distinguish a feature-associated pattern from a particular shelf position or contact surface. Move the logger between locations in documented blocks to characterize humidity; record temperature too if supported.

The key comparison is within each package: does a seam or edge repeatedly become damper than its neighboring panel? Recurrence across several packages, positions and orientations supports a material or construction contribution. Similar dampness across all regions that follows room humidity favors ambient uptake. Brief surface droplets near a temperature transition favor condensation, although construction can influence their persistence.

The method assumes that features can be consistently recognized and that dampness is observable. Differences in contents, prior exposure or package manufacture may remain unresolved. With no old-coating or uncoated reference, this study cannot isolate the new coating’s effect or establish that any feature is defective.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: The smallest falsifying check compares a repeatedly damp feature with an adjacent panel on the same package, then checks whether that contrast persists after position and orientation changes. A pattern that follows shelf contact rather than the feature weakens a material-specific explanation. No repeatable regional contrast weakens this particular mechanism but cannot exclude uniform material absorption. Report feature maps alongside environmental observations; the dry-cabinet group supplies a humidity comparator, not causal proof.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Internal moisture release: test whether the package is trapping water from inside
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Primary mechanism: moisture retained in contents, adhesive or inner paper layers migrates outward or accumulates inside a poorly ventilated package. Changing ventilation could therefore change dampness even under similar external humidity. This differs from moisture entering directly from room air; internal moisture can also produce condensation, so source and physical process must be assessed separately.

This test requires packages whose ordinary closures can be opened safely without damaging them or exposing sensitive contents. If opening is unsuitable, this alternative is not usable with the supplied resources. No chemicals, added water, customer shipments or additional measuring instruments are needed.

Record baseline dampness separately on accessible inner faces, outer panels and closures, using consistent descriptive scores. Form five pairs matched as closely as possible for initial condition and contents. Put three pairs in the dry cabinet and two in ordinary room storage. Randomly select one package in each pair to remain slightly open; keep its partner normally closed. Keep spacing and shelf contact comparable. Inspect twice daily for seven days, briefly opening closed packages only for the same short inspection interval and recording that disturbance.

Use the logger in documented blocks in each location to characterize external humidity, retaining temperature readings if available. A single logger cannot establish simultaneous conditions everywhere. Note visible droplets separately from diffuse dampness and record transfers or temperature changes.

An opening effect within both storage locations, especially with inner surfaces becoming damp first, supports trapped internal moisture as a contributor. Changes shared by open and closed packages that track storage location favor ambient uptake. Droplets associated with temperature transitions support condensation, but without surface-temperature measurements its role remains uncertain. Opening also changes drying rate for moisture originally absorbed from outside; it cannot by itself establish the moisture source.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: The smallest discriminating check is the paired open-versus-closed comparison within each location. If open packages consistently remain drier than matched closed packages, inspect whether inner-first wetting precedes that difference. Equal trajectories weaken a ventilation-limited explanation. Outer-first wetting shared across closure states favors external exposure. Report all five pair trajectories: unequal initial moisture, inspection ventilation and limited replication prevent causal proof or attribution to the new coating.

EXPAND.title: Contact-fed wetting: test whether the storage surface supplies water
EXPAND.proposal:
Primary mechanism: liquid water transfers from a damp shelf or another contacting package into paper by capillary action. Changing the contact path could change dampness even when room humidity and coating performance remain the same. This differs from paper absorbing water vapor directly from the air.

Use all ten packages in ordinary room storage for one week. At baseline, record existing stains, shelf contact points, package orientation and visible moisture on the storage surface. Form five pairs with similar initial condition and construction. Randomly place one member of each pair on its usual base and the other on a different stable face, keeping spacing comparable. Do not stack unstable packages or deliberately wet anything. Inspect the exposed shelf before placement and whenever a package is lifted. Keep the humidity logger near the packages; retain temperature readings if available.

After three days, exchange the resting faces within each pair. Photograph the original contact region and the new contact region daily, and inspect immediately before and after repositioning. Record new wetting separately from persistent old stains. The relevant change is whether fresh dampness follows the physical contact location.

This requires only the packages, existing storage surface, logger and repeated observations. It assumes packages can safely rest on alternate faces and that the suspected surface remains representative of storage. Condensation could supply water to the shelf, so contact transfer and condensation may operate together. Material absorption also controls how far transferred water spreads. A dry shelf throughout the week leaves this mechanism insufficiently challenged.
EXPAND.experiment: The smallest check is whether fresh wetness appears at the new shelf-contact region after rotation while the old region dries. Compare this with paired packages whose contact region has not yet changed. Wetting consistently remote from contact, or unchanged by repeated repositioning, weakens contact-fed wetting. A positive pattern supports a contact pathway but does not establish where the shelf water originated; ambient humidity and condensation remain competing or upstream explanations.

EXPAND.title: Moisture supplied from inside: test contents as a continuing source
EXPAND.proposal:
Primary mechanism: contents, inserts or packing materials release moisture into the package, which the paper subsequently absorbs. Reducing that internal source could reduce dampness under the same external humidity. This explanation requires filled packages with removable contents; it is unsuitable for empty samples or contents that cannot safely be handled on an ordinary bench.

Use five matched pairs of packages, matching contents and initial condition as closely as possible. Randomly select one package per pair for temporary emptying. Open both members using their normal closure, remove contents and removable inserts from the selected member, then reclose both in the same manner. Keep removed items away from the test packages. Do not open unknown, perishable or otherwise unsuitable contents. If comparable opening and reclosing are impossible, report that this test cannot be interpreted reliably.

Store all ten packages together in the room for the week, with comparable spacing and randomized positions. Log room humidity and temperature if supported. Observe daily, mapping dampness on outer faces and inspecting the interior briefly at scheduled, identical times. Record whether wetting appears first beside a particular content-contact area. Opening both groups controls part of the handling disturbance, although emptying still changes thermal mass and internal airflow.

The dry cabinet provides an optional final drying observation, but improvement there cannot by itself distinguish internal moisture from ambient absorption or condensation. The central comparison remains filled versus emptied packages sharing the same room exposure. No chemicals, shipments or deliberate wetting are needed. Contents must be sufficiently comparable for a difference to be informative; otherwise the result remains descriptive.
EXPAND.experiment: Start with one matched pair as the smallest feasibility check, then use all five pairs if handling is suitable. If emptied packages repeatedly develop less new dampness than filled comparators, an internal source becomes more plausible. Similar trajectories weaken a continuing contents-source explanation but do not exclude moisture already retained in the paper. Different thermal mass can also alter condensation, so this comparison cannot establish causal proof or isolate coating performance.

EXPAND.title: Apparent dampness: test whether coolness or surface feel drives the complaint
EXPAND.proposal:
Primary mechanism: a cool or unusually smooth surface can feel damp even without observable liquid water. Paper treatments can change texture and heat transfer, making a sensory judgment an unreliable indicator of moisture. The outcome changes if the dampness judgment disappears when packages share a common temperature history or when assessment relies on visible wetting instead of touch.

This is a second-batch alternative addressing the measurement itself. It is useful when the original complaint means “feels damp,” especially if no droplets, spreading wet patches, swelling or softening have been documented. It cannot explain clearly observed liquid water by itself.

Randomly assign five packages to the dry cabinet and five to ordinary room storage for two days. Record appearance independently of touch, using fixed descriptions of sheen, darkening, distortion and softness. Briefly touch the same small region in a consistent manner with dry hands, recording perceived coolness separately from perceived dampness. Avoid repeated rubbing. Use the logger to characterize humidity in documented blocks and record temperature if available.

Move all ten packages to adjacent positions in the room. Inspect immediately and again after several hours of shared exposure. Repeat later in the week if feasible. Common room exposure allows temperatures to approach each other, but the available equipment cannot verify surface-temperature equality. It can also change actual moisture content, which limits interpretation.

The resources are the ten packages, logger, cabinet and room. No extra instruments or chemicals are required. Material-dependent feel, ambient moisture uptake and condensation can coexist; this alternative checks whether the reported endpoint is specific enough to distinguish them.
EXPAND.experiment: The smallest check compares immediate tactile ratings with later ratings and visible signs for the same packages, using room-stationary packages as comparators. Dampness ratings that track coolness and fade without any visible change support a sensory contribution. Persistent wet patches, droplets or progressive softening weaken a purely sensory explanation. Because invisible absorbed water may also change during equilibration, report this as a check on the reliability of “feels damp,” not proof that the packages are dry.

EXPAND.title: Residue deliquescence: test whether localized deposits attract liquid water
EXPAND.proposal:
Primary mechanism: hygroscopic residues on a package can absorb atmospheric water and, above a composition-dependent relative humidity, dissolve into a concentrated liquid film. This could produce localized dampness without a general failure of the coating. Possible residues include manufacturing or handling deposits; their presence and identity are hypotheses, not established facts. The outcome would change if wet patches repeatedly appeared at particular deposit sites during humid periods and diminished during dry storage.

This approach requires visible or otherwise recognizable suspect areas and naturally occurring humidity variation. It uses ten packages, the logger, the dry cabinet and ordinary room storage for one week. No chemicals, added water, scraping, deliberate humidification or customer shipments are needed. Inspect without touching or smelling unknown deposits.

Number the packages and map any existing specks, rings, crystalline-looking deposits or localized films. Record nearby apparently clean regions as within-package comparators. If no suspect sites exist, this approach has little discriminatory value. Match packages approximately by initial condition, then randomly allocate one member of each pair to room storage and the other to the cabinet. Inspect the mapped regions twice daily for four days, then exchange locations and continue through day seven. Keep spacing and shelf contact comparable.

Place the logger near the room samples during the main observation periods and characterize cabinet humidity in documented blocks. Retain temperature readings if supported; one logger cannot provide simultaneous exposure records for both locations.

A repeatable association between particular deposits and localized wet films would support a residue contribution. General paper darkening would fit ambient absorption better; rapid droplets after a temperature transition would favor condensation. These mechanisms can coexist. Visual observations cannot identify a chemical residue, establish a precise humidity threshold or distinguish every residue from a coating component.
EXPAND.experiment: The smallest check compares each suspect site with an adjacent apparently clean area and with similarly positioned regions on other packages. Look for fresh wetting during ordinary humid periods, disappearance in the cabinet and recurrence at the same sites after return. If clean and suspect areas change together, or wetting consistently appears elsewhere, the deposit-specific explanation loses support. If humidity barely varies, the week is inconclusive. Even repeated localization is bounded evidence, because local construction, surface temperature and prior damage remain possible explanations; it does not prove contamination or coating failure.
